summary: A response to RFC 1550 submitted to the IETF IPng area by the Electric Power Research Institute, giving its comments on IPng. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A power industry research group shares what it wants from the next Internet.

subtitle: The electric power industry's view: unified standards for the information superhighway.

tldr.problem: The Internet and competing standard suites (OSI, proprietary protocols) create fragmentation; a unified approach is needed.
tldr.mechanism: IPng should be designed following established international standards processes and should support industrial-grade reliability for critical infrastructure like power systems.
tldr.outcome: The power industry sees IPng as an opportunity to move everyone toward a single transport infrastructure, but believes OSI-based solutions are more suitable than pure TCP/IP.

today: RFC 1673 is Informational from August 1994. IPv6, as standardized, retained the IETF process and did not follow the OSI model that EPRI preferred. However, the power industry eventually adopted IPv6 widely, as it proved stable and scalable despite its origins outside formal international standards bodies.

sections.title: EPRI's Position on IPng
sections.content:
The Electric Power Research Institute, a non-profit research organization with 700 utility members, submitted RFC 1673 to the IETF IPng area. EPRI represents the electric power industry's needs. The RFC argues that the choice of IPng is critical to building a national information infrastructure comparable to past basic standards like railways and electricity itself.

EPRI acknowledges that the power industry is a heavy user of the Internet Protocol Suite, but notes that its long-term strategy is based on formal international standards (ISO, CCITT, IEEE, ANSI) rather than the more informal IETF process. EPRI has developed the Utility Communications Architecture (UCA) specification and the Industry Government Open Systems Specification (IGOSS), both based on OSI protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The power industry uses the Internet today, but prefers carefully vetted international standards because they need things to be very reliable and predictable.

sections.title: Engineering Considerations
sections.content:
EPRI's mandatory requirement is that IPng provide industrial-strength computing and communications for upper-layer OSI applications. Transport mechanisms like RFC 1006 (TCP/IP over OSI) are only acceptable as a transition strategy, not as a long-term solution.

Basic requirements include scaleability with an essentially unlimited address space (20 octets or larger, well beyond IPv4's 32 bits), routing table economy in very large networks, and support for existing Internet and OSI applications. Key engineering considerations emphasize using available, mature, internationally agreed standards with off-the-shelf implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The power industry needs addresses that can grow forever, fast routing in huge networks, and the ability to use proven standards that are already implemented in real products.

sections.title: A Pragmatic Solution
sections.content:
EPRI proposes an evolutionary transition using OSI rather than a revolutionary change. A dual-network-layer strategy should allow operation without modifying existing inter-domain routing, while supporting proprietary protocols (IPX, AppleTalk) and other addressing schemes (X.121, E.164).

Additional requirements include route aggregation and service selection for routing effectiveness, flexible administration that can be geographically based or carrier-based, simplified configuration, and dynamic addressing to minimize manual intervention. The standard should support multi-homed hosts and applications, not just interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The new Internet should work alongside existing networks, support different addressing styles, and let organizations set it up flexibly for their own needs.

sections.title: EPRI's Vision
sections.content:
EPRI emphasizes that multiple competing standards cannot be sustained indefinitely—just as railways needed a uniform gauge. The organization sees IPng as an ideal opportunity to create a unified transport superhighway but believes convergence should happen through formal, internationally accepted standards rather than proprietary innovation.

EPRI also highlights the need for convergent standards efforts in security, directory services, network management, and real-time application support.
sections.plainLanguage: One standard is better than many, and that standard should come from careful international agreement, not just one organization's innovation.
